title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6625 – Reuters estimate
body: Earlier, some important news: China's central bank, regulators to meet on stock support after record 12-week slide - The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.

title: BTCPay Server tells operators to shut down after reports of hot wallets being drained
body: BTCPay Server, the open-source software many merchants use to accept Bitcoin payments without a third-party processor, has told operators to shut down their instances after receiving reports that hot wallets on multiple servers were being drained by unauthorized attackers. --- Adding to concerens re the drain last week: investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: Binance hack shakes crypto --- In a post on X, the project asked anyone running an instance to take it offline with its shutdown command until the investigation is complete. BTCPay has not yet disclosed the cause of the attack, how many servers were affected or how much was taken. A hot wallet is one whose private keys sit on an internet-connected server, so it can send funds automatically, for example to pay out refunds. That convenience makes it a bigger target than offline storage. The incident involves software built around Bitcoin, not the Bitcoin network itself. The warning follows two recent security events at the project. On October 29, BTCPay released emergency version 2.4.7 to fix one critical and several medium-risk vulnerabilities. In August, attackers exploited a separate flaw to steal Lightning Network credentials and drain nodes running behind BTCPay, including one operated by hardware wallet maker Foundation. At that time, BTCPay said its standard on-chain wallets, including hot wallets created inside the software, were not affected.

title: Market playbook: Can the RBA surprise markets again and give AUD/USD another reason to rally?
body: The aussie will be hoping that Christmas will come early this year with the RBA perhaps delivering a timely present tomorrow. But with markets already well expecting a rate hike this week, will Bullock have anything left in her bag of tricks to give the aussie another leg higher? As things stand, traders are pricing in roughly 87% odds of a 25 bps rate hike tomorrow, which will take the cash rate to 4.85%. And this will follow the rate hike from September, with inflation proving to be a rather stubborn headache to deal with for policymakers. But looking further out, traders are barely pricing in any further tightening beyond the one expected tomorrow. In fact, traders only see around 33 bps of cumulative rate hikes by June 2027 and that includes the expected move this week. Essentially, that is signaling a one more and done move by the RBA. So, could the central bank catch traders off guard given the backdrop ahead of tomorrow? I would argue that it's not outside of the realms of possibility as the central bank will want to retain as much flexibility and optionality as they can, as do all major central banks these days. The more hawkish scenario would be a 25 bps hike accompanied by stronger warnings on inflation and a clear indication that further tightening remains firmly on the table. And if Bullock explicitly pushes back against expectations of an extended pause, that could force traders to rethink the rate outlook.

That's a big miss on German retail sales with consumption activity softening across the board. Looking at the breakdown, sales at petrol stations were down 3.4%, sales of food products down 1.4%, and non-food retail trade was down 2.4% in September compared to the month before. That is hardly a convincing sign that German households are dealing well with the growing inflation pressure that is tiding over Europe especially in the second half of the year. The only bright spot is that perhaps with the new temporary fuel tax relief, running from October to December, that could prop up petrol station sales. So, we'll wait and see on that. But overall, the decline across broader categories is signaling that the health of the German consumer is not doing well. Households are definitely feeling the pinch of higher price pressures and that is showing up in their spending activity/pattern. As such, that just adds another troubling sign for the ECB as the central bank is in a tight spot to balance between flagging growth conditions and higher inflation across the euro area heading into year-end.

title: US midterms 2026: Is Trump about to lose his grip on Congress?
body: I reckon that US president Trump might be in for a rude awakening after tomorrow. Or perhaps he is already aware of his current predicament, although I wouldn't put it past him to refuse to accept that reality. Either way, he's going to have to deal with the possibility that his grip on Congress could be slipping away. As the US heads to the polls tomorrow, both the control of the House and Senate hang in the balance. And if the latest polls are anything to go by, Republicans have plenty of reasons to be nervous. The national generic congressional ballot polls show Democrats holding a sizeable lead over Republicans as cost-of-living frustrations and dissatisfaction with Trump's presidency have weighed on sentiment. Having said that, the national polling doesn't necessarily translate neatly into congressional seats. So, what does this mean for markets? Let's start with a bit of backdrop. Democrats need a net gain of three seats in the House and four in the Senate to wrest control of both chambers from Republicans. If Republicans lose the House, then Trump's legislative agenda could essentially run into a brick wall. As for Democrats, that would open the door to more investigations and tougher negotiations over government spending, taxation and funding. But what if Democrats take both chambers? Well, that would certainly tighten the screws further especially when it comes to Trump's judicial appointments and other nominations requiring Senate confirmation.

The shift also changes what traders will watch: the overnight rate, not the seven-day rate, now looks set to become the signal of PBOC intent, so any future adjustment to the 1.25% level will be read as a policy move. With October PMIs in contraction and equities coming off their worst month in more than a decade, a cleaner transmission channel gives Beijing a sharper tool if it decides to lower borrowing costs. For the yuan, the change is structural rather than directional, but it modernises a framework global investors have long found opaque. --- China is quietly swapping out the dial it uses to steer interest rates, trading a seven-day benchmark for an overnight one that brings its monetary toolkit closer to the Fed's than ever before.

title: Gold Technicals: Gold is up sharply erasing some of last week's declines. Bounces off key MA target.
body: Lower yields help gold recover Gold fell sharply Friday as risk-off sentiment dominated trading. Today, the focus has shifted toward lower Treasury yields, helping gold recover some of that decline. The U.S. 10-year yield is down 5.0 basis points at 4.87%. Gold typically benefits from falling yields because it pays no interest. When bonds offer a lower return, the opportunity cost of holding gold falls, making the metal relatively more attractive. The rebound is also getting help from a successful test of a key technical support level. Buyers lean against the 100-week moving average On the weekly chart, gold tested its 100-week moving average at $3882.35 (see blue line on the chart above). Today's low slipped just below that level before buyers stepped in and pushed the price higher. Gold is now trading near $3968, just below the session high of $3970.34. The bounce reinforces the importance of the 100-week moving average as a longer-term barometer. As long as the price remains above it, buyers who leaned against that level can stay in the game. A move back below would undermine the rebound and give sellers more control. Reclaimed swing area provides close support Today's recovery has also taken gold back above the swing area between $3942 and $3959. That zone defined a series of swing lows from June 24 through July 17 before giving way during Friday's tumble (see red numbered circles on the chart above). Moving back above the area is a positive step for buyers.

title: U.S. stocks rebound as Iran diplomacy hopes and lower oil outweigh mixed economic data
body: Today's U.S. economic data gave buyers and sellers something to work with. Manufacturing continues to expand, but a sharp decline in construction spending and stubborn inflation pressures cloud the broader outlook. The data lean mildly bullish for manufacturing activity, but offer a less convincing signal for stocks. The stronger bullish influence is coming from the Middle East, where renewed hopes for U.S.–Iran diplomacy and sharply lower oil prices are helping buyers regain some control after a difficult October. ISM manufacturing strengthens, but price pressures remain elevated The ISM manufacturing report provided the strongest growth signal. The headline index rose to 55.5 from 54.5, beating expectations near 54.6–54.7. Production increased to 59.0 from 56.7, while new orders edged higher to 55.5 from 55.3. Employment slipped to 52.4 from 52.7 but remained above the 50 expansion barometer. Manufacturing continues to grow, although hiring lost a little momentum. On inflation, ISM prices paid fell to 75.2 from 77.9. That is encouraging at the margin, but the level still points to widespread input-price increases. Supplier deliveries also slowed further. The report gives the growth bulls support, but offers the Fed little reason to declare victory on inflation. S&P Global PMI signals slower growth and pressure on margins The S&P Global report tempered some of that optimism. Its final October manufacturing PMI fell to 54.9 from September's 55.9, below expectations for 56.0.

Manufacturers responded with the largest increases in selling prices in more than four years. Confidence in the outlook remained historically subdued.

title: US election: The key races that could tip control of Congress
body: Tuesday's midterm elections will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress or Democrats gain the ability to slow President Donald Trump's agenda during the final two years of his term (and cause other headaches for President Trump). The numbers are straightforward: Democrats need a net gain of three House seats to reach the 218-seat majority threshold. In the Senate, Republicans hold a 53–47 advantage. Democrats need four net gains to reach 51, as a 50–50 split would leave Republicans in control through Vice President JD Vance's tie-breaking vote. Senate: The Republican seats Democrats need to flip North Carolina and Maine are central to the Democratic path. In North Carolina, former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper faces Republican Michael Whatley for retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis's seat. In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins faces Democrat Troy Jackson. Collins's ability to attract crossover voters is especially important in a state Kamala Harris carried in 2024. Ohio and Texas could provide decisive gains. Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is challenging Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio's special election. In Texas, Republican Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico in a closely watched contest after defeating incumbent John Cornyn in the primary. Both races test whether Democrats can win statewide in territory that has favored Republicans. Alaska, Iowa and Kansas provide additional routes.

title: Oil prices sink as Iran's President says Supreme Leader granted certain authorities regarding negotiations
body: Iran's President Pezeshkian said the Supreme Leader has granted the government certain authorities regarding negotiations, according to the state-run ISNA news agency. The markets are taking this as a signal for greater flexibility and potentially strengthen the government's ability to reach a deal with the US. As a reminder, strategic decisions remain under the authority of the Supreme Leader, so any progress requires alignment between the Supreme Leader and negotiators. Iran has already proposed a two-day framework to reopen the Strait of Hormuz conditional to its demands being met, which include the lifting of the blockade, the release of frozen funds and sactions relief among others. This a shorter timeline that the seven-day framework proposed a month ago. The markets interpreted the shortened timeline as a positive development, although the US has not accepted the proposal yet and negotiations continue. It shouldn't be surprising to see other markets respond positively to the news as lower oil prices would reduce inflation and rate hike bets, and at the same time improve growth expectations. Precious metals, for example, jumped on the headline on expectations that a deal would lower significantly oil prices and trigger a dovish repricing in rate hike bets. The stock market found support as lower oil prices and a less hawkish Fed would lead to improving growth outlook.

title: Nasdaq trims losses as renewed hopes for US-Iran deal improve the risk sentiment ahead of the midterms
body: The Nasdaq sold off sharply last week driven primarily by AI-related and technology stocks. Concerns about the profitability of massive AI investments, disappointing corporate earnings and rising financing costs triggered a sharp rotation away from Big Tech. Investors started to question whether the enormous amounts being invested in AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns to justify the expenditure. Keep in mind that AI investment became a significant contributor to US economic growth, so a prolonged reduction in spending could negatively affect the broader economy. The selloff, though, started weeks ago as macro and geopolitical headwinds intensified. The higher-than-expected inflation data raised concerns about a more extended tightening cycle, while renewed US-Iran tensions weighed on growth expectations as oil prices surged. This came at a time of overcrowded positioning. Looking ahead, the focus will be on US-Iran negotiations and the US midterm elections. The risk sentiment improved a bit after Iran proposed over the weekend a two-day framework to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for US concessions, including sanctions relief, the release of frozen assets and lift of the blockade. This is a shorter timeline that the seven-day framework proposed a month ago. The markets interpreted the shortened timeline as a positive development, although the US has not accepted the proposal yet and negotiations continue.

title: Morning Kickstart: Oil tumbles as Iran talks continue. USD mixed ahead of ISM
body: November trading begins with a sharp decline in crude oil and another round of headlines surrounding negotiations between the US and Iran. The overnight/weekend reports point to continued diplomatic engagement, but conditions surrounding sanctions and the reopening of the Strait remain significant hurdles. Iranian negotiators left Doha on Sunday, although sources said their departure was not due to difficulties in the negotiations. A draft proposal has been circulated for feedback, and a follow-up meeting remains possible. Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Baghaei said messages continue to be exchanged and that the US must make a decision. He described the issues as complex and presented Iran's willingness to compress implementation of its seven-day proposal into two days as a sign of goodwill. However, Iran also maintains that the Strait cannot reopen before US sanctions are lifted. Separately, Kyodo reported that a senior Iranian official linked reopening to US acceptance of seven conditions. The official suggested Iran could adopt a more flexible position on the nuclear issue if an agreement on reopening the Strait is reached. For traders, continued talks keep the possibility of an agreement alive. The conditions attached to those talks leave plenty of room for another shift in expectations. Neverthless, oil is starting the week sharply lower, but the headlines have yet to deliver a confirmed agreement. The dollar is mixed.

title: Why being right but being early is the same as being wrong
body: One of the most famous quotes in financial markets comes from economist John Maynard Keynes "markets can remain irrational longer than you can stay solvent".It captures one of the most important lessons in trading: being fundamentally correct does not necessarily mean making money. Traders often identify situations where asset prices appear disconnected from fundamentals. A stock may look overvalued or a currency may be excessively strong. However, recognising a mispricing and successfully trading it are two different things. Imagine a traders believes a stock is significantly overvalued and decides to short it at $100, expecting it to fall towards $80. Instead, the stock continues rising to $120 or even $140, despite no meaningful improvement in its fundamentals. The traders might eventually be proven right, but that doesn't mean he will survive long enough to benefit from the correction. This is especially dangerous when leverage is involved. Borrowed capital amplifies both gains and losses, meaning even relatively small adverse price movements can trigger margin calls or forced liquidations. Leverage effectively reduces the amount of time a traders has to be right. Markets are not driven exclusively by fundamentals. Expectations, positioning and momentum can overpower fundamentals, especially over shorter time horizons. An asset with weak fundamentals can continue rising if markets are heavily positioned for further gains.

title: 24/7 Markets: Are Brokers Ready?
body: Financial markets have long run on fixed trading sessions. Those hours have shaped how brokers manage instrument availability, client support, liquidity, and risk. That pattern is loosening. More products can now be traded outside standard sessions, while selected instruments offer 24/7 market access. For brokers, the change opens room to widen what they offer and meet shifting client demand. It also raises a practical question: what happens when trading continues past the hours the underlying market normally keeps? Offering an instrument is the straightforward part. The harder part is everything behind it: pricing, institutional liquidity, how orders are filled and the operations that support them. The question is no longer only what clients can trade, but whether a broker's own setup is ready for a market that no longer follows the old timetable. Availability is becoming part of the proposition Client expectations move with access. Once an instrument can be traded outside standard sessions, clients begin to treat that flexibility as normal, and availability becomes part of what a broker is judged on. That turns a product decision into an operational one. Extending access can answer real demand, but every instrument has its own characteristics and trading terms. A round-the-clock offering in one product category says nothing about whether another market can, or should, work the same way.

title: Bitcoin rebounds after the Binance hack driven selloff as US-Iran deal hopes improve risk sentiment
body: Bitcoin sold off sharply towards the end of last week following the news of the Binance security breach, which reportedly resulted in approximately $6.3 billion being drained from multiple wallets. The hack, described as the largest cryptocurrency heist in history, raised concerns about exchange security and potential contagion across the broader crypto ecosystem. Although Binance pledged to cover customer losses, the uncertainty surrounding the stolen assets and the potential for further liquidations weighed heavily on sentiment. Around $1.53 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated over 24 hours, amplifying the initial selloff as forced liquidations accelerated the downside. However, Bitcoin eventually rebounded as concerns surrounding the hack gradually eased. Binance's commitment to cover customer losses helped contain fears of broader contagion, while improving sentiment around US-Iran negotiations provided additional support to the crypto market. Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days strengthened hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough, reducing some of the geopolitical risk premium weighing on markets, with oil prices erasing most of last week's gains. Nevertheless, the macro backdrop remains challenging, with inflation risks, growth concerns, Fed rate hikes and geopolitical uncertainty continuing to limit the upside. We will likely need a breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations or dovish Fed comments to change the current bearish trend.

title: European Natural Gas Prices Plunge 10%
body: European natural gas prices dropped 10% to €93/MWh on Monday, marking their sharpest decline since April 8, as renewed optimism over potential US-Iran talks eased fears of disruptions to Middle Eastern energy supplies. Iran's supreme leader has reportedly authorized the government to engage in negotiations, following reports that President Donald Trump is inclined to allow more time for diplomacy. The pullback erased part of last week's surge, which had driven prices above €100/MWh for the first time since 2022, with geopolitical tensions adding a substantial risk premium. Despite the recent decline, supply risks persist as colder weather approaches and storage levels remain below target. Germany's gas reserves were only 61.03% full as of November 2, well short of the government's 70% target, while EU-wide storage was under 75%, a historically low level. Forecasts indicate temperatures 2°C to 4°C below seasonal norms in major German cities, with freezing conditions likely in the country's southern and eastern regions.
